name: Bazel
baseline: GNU Make 4.3 with default built-in rules (also measured: Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables, and Ninja 1.11.1, both of which beat Bazel)
workload: Third-party overhead benchmark: N simulated modules (50 to 100,000) whose build rules only touch 0-byte files, measured as full build, incremental build (a few files changed) and null build (nothing changed), parallelism 4.
claimed_speedup: Bazel's own README claims only 'fast and incremental builds' (no numbers). Third-party table, x86_64, 100,000 modules: incremental build Bazel 61.911 s vs recursive Make (default rules) 692.201 s and single Make 292.019 s (about 11x and 4.7x, derived from page data); null build Bazel 20.193 s vs 688.101 s and 285.583 s (about 34x and 14x, derived from page data). At 5,000 modules: incremental 4.040 s vs 22.408 s / 24.813 s; null 1.091 s vs 22.236 s / 24.473 s. NEGATIVE results in the same table: Ninja is faster at every size (100,000 modules: incremental 10.358 s, null 7.073 s, full 407.131 s vs Bazel 61.911 s, 20.193 s, 1381.402 s), Make run with --no-builtin-rules is also faster than Bazel for incremental and null builds (9.486 s and 7.816 s recursive at 100,000 modules), and Bazel's full build is slower than every Make and Ninja variant (e.g. 82.779 s vs 28.723 s Make and 6.079 s Ninja at 5,000 modules).
compiler_and_flags: No compiler involved (rules touch 0-byte files); tools run with no arguments plus Make with --no-builtin-rules --no-builtin-variables; GNU Make 4.3, Ninja 1.11.1, Bazel 8.0.1 on the Arm runs, Bazel version recorded as 'no_version' on the x86_64 runs.
hardware: x86_64 run: 4 CPUs, 7G RAM, Linux 6.8.0-48-generic (Ubuntu 22.04); Arm run: aarch64 4 CPUs, 7G, Linux 6.8.0-1018-raspi (kernel name suggests a Raspberry Pi); CPU model not stated; runs dated 2025-02-10/11
tradeoffs: JVM server process: 350 to 500 MB resident in these runs and 310 MB to 1 GB of output-base disk even for empty modules; slow cold full build; steep learning curve (BUILD/Starlark files, many options); hermetic sandboxed actions with remote cache and remote execution, whose benefits this benchmark does not exercise. Output lands in the user cache directory, not the source tree.
caveats: The benchmark is synthetic and measures pure build-tool overhead: no compiler runs, so it says nothing about real C or C++ compile and link wall-clock time or about remote caching and execution, which are Bazel's main speed levers. Bazel only wins against Make run with default built-in rules (the benchmark's own results show Make drops to Ninja-like times with --no-builtin-rules) and only on incremental builds from about 5,000 modules and null builds from about 1,000 modules (on Arm at 1,000 modules Make is still faster); at small sizes (50 to 100 modules) Bazel's full build is about 10 to 22 s vs 0.04 to 0.23 s for Ninja and Make, and Ninja beats Bazel in every row. The measurement is by a single maintainer repo with 5 stars (GPL-3.0 benchmark code, last commit 2025-02-28); CPU model is not stated, so it cannot be tier A. The Bazel version is not recorded on the x86_64 runs. The Bazel repo itself carries no Make or Ninja comparison; the Bazel 'fast' claim is first-party and unquantified.

name: Ninja
baseline: GNU Make (CMake Unix Makefiles generator backend)
workload: Meson author's experiment: 1000 generated trivial C files (each defining one function and including a header) built into one executable with CMake, once with its Make backend and once with its Ninja backend, four parallel processes, fastest of several runs; plus an anecdote about no-op builds of the Clang compiler.
claimed_speedup: Switching the CMake backend from Make to Ninja shaves 3.5 seconds (over 20%) off the total build time of the 1000-file project with no CMake file changes. Anecdote on the same page: no-op build times of 30 seconds for Make versus less than one second for Ninja when compiling the Clang compiler. The bar-chart values are images, so only these two text figures are quotable.
hardware: 2011-era MacBook Pro running Ubuntu 13.04 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Deliberately has no build-file features (no conditionals, no built-in rules, no globbing); build.ninja files are meant to be emitted by a generator such as CMake or Meson, so Ninja alone is not a replacement for a hand-written Makefile. It needs a generator step. Uses all hardware threads by default; the manual says the design trades convenience for speed.
caveats: The only quantified third-party comparison reachable is written by the author of Meson, a competing build system, and is old (2011 hardware, Ubuntu 13.04); CPU model, GNU Make version, compiler and flags are not stated, the generator script is not on the page, and the per-build-system numbers are in images that were not readable here. The 30 s versus under 1 s Clang figure is explicitly anecdotal. First-party claim on the Ninja manual page (https://github.com/ninja-build/ninja/blob/master/doc/manual.asciidoc, introduction): Chromium, with over 30,000 source files, had other build systems, including one built from custom non-recursive Makefiles, that took ten seconds to start building after changing one file, while Ninja takes under a second; no hardware, date or method is given there, so it is tier C on its own. The CMake Best Practices lead for this project gives no timing for Ninja. Ninja's advantage is mostly incremental and no-op startup time; clean full builds are compiler-bound, and the 20 percent gain is on a synthetic project of trivial files, so real projects will see less on clean builds.

name: doctest
workload: bench.py-generated CMake projects built single-threaded: (1) 201 source files with the framework header included in every file, (2) 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts across 10 files, (3) a runtime loop of 10 million passing CHECK(i == i) asserts, with and without INFO(i) logging.
claimed_speedup: Header cost: doctest.h costs 11ms-23ms per source file against 380ms-470ms for catch.hpp (page: more than 36 times lighter on MSVC). 201 files with header everywhere, Linux GCC Release: 11.05s vs 99.48s (baselines 4.29s vs 4.50s); MSVC Release: 8.71s vs 87.17s. 50k CHECK(a==b) asserts, Linux GCC Release: 257.40s vs 608.94s; MSVC Release: 58.73s vs 448.68s (page: between 0 and 8 times faster than Catch); with DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS 97.46s on Linux GCC Release. Runtime 10M asserts: MSVC Release 0.40s vs 0.76s, Linux GCC Release 0.29s vs 0.29s, Linux Clang Release 0.28s vs 0.32s; with INFO logging Linux GCC Release 0.52s vs 3.60s (page: around 20% faster for plain asserts, a few times faster with logging).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2017 15.8.1, MinGW GCC 8.1.0, Linux GCC 6.3.0, Linux Clang 4.0.0. scripts/bench/bench.py configures CMake with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug or Release (CMake default flags), adds -std=c++11 on non-MSVC and -w on GCC/Clang; no explicit -O flags; builds single-threaded with cmake --build.
hardware: Intel i7 3770k, 16G RAM; Windows 7 on an SSD, and Ubuntu 17.04 in a VirtualBox VM on a HDD
tradeoffs: Smaller feature set than Catch2 (modelled on Catch; the FAQ lists the differences, not read). The biggest assert-compile wins need the non-decomposing CHECK_EQ(a,b) form and the DOCTEST_CONFIG_SUPER_FAST_ASSERTS define, so they are not like-for-like with Catch's CHECK(a==b). DOCTEST_CONFIG_DISABLE strips tests from the binary. Single header, C++11.
caveats: The project's own benchmark (Dec 2018): doctest 2.2.0 against Catch 2.3.0, both far behind current releases; Catch2 v3 became a compiled library with a different compile-time profile and was not measured. Flags come from the public script rather than the page text, and there are no explicit optimisation flags. Linux numbers come from a VirtualBox VM on a HDD; no repeat counts or variance are given. Runtime for plain asserts is near parity on GCC and Clang Release (0.29s vs 0.29s); the large runtime win is only with INFO logging. README says compile time is better 'by orders of magnitude', while the tables show roughly 9-10x on whole-build header cost and up to about 8x on assert macros. Google Test and Boost.Test are not benchmarked on the page. The tier A rating rests on the public script plus stated compilers and CPU; a verifier may still downgrade it for the missing explicit flags.

name: clcache
baseline: uncached MSVC compile (cl.exe without a compiler cache)
workload: OpenMW GitLab CI job (MSBuild, MSVC 2022, 64-bit RelWithDebInfo) run uncached versus with a third-party fork of clcache and a CI-restored cache across successive pipeline runs.
claimed_speedup: Merge request text: the average uncached MSBuild RelWithDebInfo job is either barely passing or barely failing the 2 hour timeout; with the clcache fork the 2nd build (partial cache) succeeded in 100 minutes, the 3rd build (full cache) in 55 minutes, and subsequent jobs in as little as 49 minutes. Roughly 2.2x (120 / 55, derived from page data, the 120 minute figure being the job timeout, not a measured uncached time).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 2022, 64-bit, RelWithDebInfo; clcache with CLCACHE_COMPRESS, cache limit 1.5 GB (clcache -M 1610612736)
tradeoffs: Python wrapper around cl.exe (the repo also has a pyinstaller folder) that stores compiler output in a local directory cache; the optional clcachesrv.py server is documented as greatly improving the performance of cache hits. Upstream is archived: Python 3.10+ and MSVC 2019+ patches live only in forks, which is why users run forks. Precompiled-header caching is not available upstream (the OpenMW fork author says his fork has experimental changes toward it).
caveats: The README and CHANGELOG of frerich/clcache carry no timing numbers (only 'greatly improves performance of cache hits' for the server). The only reachable numbers are third-party CI anecdotes. The OpenMW merge request (opened 2025-11-29) used Aussiemon's fork pinned to a commit, not upstream, and states no uncached time (only that it is near the 2 hour timeout), no runner hardware, and mixes cache states across different pipeline runs, so the speedup is approximate and not a controlled comparison. The upstream issue https://github.com/frerich/clcache/issues/251 (2016, Windows Server 2012 R2, E5-2650) reports the opposite: a 5 to 8 minute build rose to 23 minutes with a cold cache and was roughly equal to no clcache when fully cached, blamed on cache lock contention and virus scanning. The same MR author found ccache's MSVC precompiled-header hits as slow as misses and called clcache the most stable option, but wished ccache could match its speed.

Samba 3.0.20: 314.0s local, 101.8s plain (about 3.1x, derived), 31.4s pump (about 10x, derived). glibc 2.6: 946.4s local, 534.0s plain, 357.8s pump. binutils 2.18: 125.8s local, 35.4s plain, 28.7s pump. httpd 2.0.43: 139.8s local, 85.1s plain, 80.1s pump. Page text: pump mode is sometimes more than 3x faster than plain distcc (Samba), and up to 2.5x faster than non-pump on 4-processor clients for large Google projects. hello-2.1.1 gets slower: 0.7s local, 0.9s plain, 1.1s pump.
hardware: Client: 2.8GHz Intel Pentium 4, 2G RAM, Linux 2.6.18.5 (modified Ubuntu 6.06). Servers: 38 machines described as 4 CPU 2GHz AMD Dual Core Processor 270 with 2G RAM (152 CPUs in total).
stars_or_usage: 2.3k stars; README says it has compiled the Linux kernel, KDE, GNOME and Samba, and run with hundreds of servers
tradeoffs: Needs the distccd daemon and a compatible compiler on every volunteer machine and a fast network (a slow network can cancel the gain). Plain mode ships preprocessed source and still preprocesses on the client; pump mode needs identical system headers on client and servers, assumes sources and headers do not change during the build, and falls back to plain distcc when it hits an error (the page says the Linux kernel needed special handling). Small projects get slower (hello-2.1.1). README.pump says pump mode will probably show no major gain with fewer than about ten CPUs. GPL licence.
caveats: First-party Google/distcc page dated 2008 (copyright line) on 2008-era hardware; compiler version and flags are not stated, so not tier A even though the harness lives in the repo (bench/ directory, contents not read). The local baseline is one single-core 2.8GHz Pentium 4 against 152 server CPUs, which inflates the ratio; the page itself says a multi-processor client would show smaller gains. Only make time is counted, not configure. The page notes pump runs that silently fell back to plain mode while collecting results. The ratios above marked derived are computed from the page's wall-time column. README.md separately claims three machines are 2.6 times faster than one and README.pump says pump mode is up to 10X faster than plain distcc for the compile step (not the whole build); neither number is on the benchmark page. No comparison with ccache, icecream or a modern build system.

name: TCC (Tiny C Compiler)
baseline: GCC (gcc 16.2.1 at default -O0, with -Wall -Wextra); also Clang 22.1.8 at default -O0
workload: Generated single translation unit of 200 x 200 = 40,000 synthetic arithmetic functions in C; per-function minimum time of syntax check, compile-to-object, and full build with link.
claimed_speedup: Build [us/f]: tcc 0.9.28rc 2.6 vs gcc 16.2.1 500.7 vs clang 22.1.8 60.3; Compile [us/f]: tcc 3.5 vs gcc 732.5 vs clang 123.3; Check [us/f]: tcc 2.9 vs gcc 18.2 vs clang 15.4. About 190x faster than gcc and 23x faster than clang on full build (derived from page data). Project README: 'Compiles and links about 10 times faster than gcc -O0.'
compiler_and_flags: tcc built with no flags (check/compile use -c); gcc and clang invoked with -Wall -Wextra plus -fsyntax-only, -c or nothing, i.e. default optimization (-O0), per the public benchmark script; tcc 0.9.28rc, gcc 16.2.1, clang 22.1.8
hardware: AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 (8+8) @ 5.09 GHz, Arch Linux, 2026-09
tradeoffs: Single-pass compiler with no optimizer: generated code is unoptimized (similar to gcc -O0), so it suits compile-and-run scripting, bootstrapping and fast edit cycles but not performance-critical builds. Supports i386, x86_64, arm, aarch64, riscv64 and has an optional bounds checker. Does not support C++.
caveats: The benchmark is synthetic (one huge TU of arithmetic call chains, no #include or header parsing); its own README says real-world build times are dominated by headers and linking, so the ~190x gap overstates typical gains (the project claims about 10x vs gcc -O0, and a 2003-era Links browser comparison of 2.27 s vs 20.0 s on GCC 3.2 appears only in search snippets because bellard.org was blocked). gcc and clang are compared at their default -O0, not at -O2, so the win is against unoptimized builds only. In this run the produced binaries' run time was 113 us/f for tcc vs 98 for gcc and 155 for clang, but run time is measured on the same synthetic code. The benchmark author is a third party (nordlow), but the suite is a single-maintainer repo with 166 stars; the tcc check row uses -c so it also emits object code unlike gcc -fsyntax-only. License: COPYING is LGPL-2.1; a RELICENSING file lists authors agreeing to MIT-style terms, but the whole tree is not relicensed.
